summary: A duodenal villus cut lengthwise, cell by cell: simple columnar enterocytes with a brush border, scattered goblet cells and a few intraepithelial lymphocytes, all resting on a basement membrane around a core of lamina propria.
clinical: Gluten-driven immune injury flattens the villi (villous atrophy), deepens the crypts and raises the number of intraepithelial lymphocytes; duodenal biopsy is the diagnostic standard, and increased lymphocytes are the earliest change.
Lactase is a brush-border enzyme of the enterocytes, so its genetic decline in adults or loss after mucosal injury leaves lactose undigested, causing bloating and osmotic diarrhoea.

SubTool-1.name: Enterocytes
SubTool-1.description: Tall simple columnar absorptive cells with oval, basally placed nuclei and a brush border of microvilli (the rough apical surface). The brush border carries digestive enzymes such as disaccharidases and peptidases; the duodenum is the main site of iron absorption.

SubTool-2.name: Goblet cells
SubTool-2.description: Pale, mucin-filled cells scattered among the enterocytes, each with a small nucleus squeezed into its narrow base. They secrete the mucus that protects and lubricates the surface, and become steadily more numerous from the duodenum toward the colon.

SubTool-4.name: Intraepithelial lymphocytes
SubTool-4.description: Small round cells with a dense nucleus lying between the enterocytes, above the basement membrane. They are mainly CD8+ T cells that police the epithelium; normally there are fewer than about 25 per 100 enterocytes, and a rise is the earliest biopsy sign of coeliac disease.

SubTool-0.name: Basement membrane
SubTool-0.description: The thin sheet that every enterocyte and goblet cell rests on, shaped as a sleeve around the villus core. It separates the simple columnar epithelium from the lamina propria, and absorbed nutrients cross it to reach the villus capillaries and lacteal.

SubTool-3.name: Lamina propria
SubTool-3.description: The loose connective tissue core of the villus, shown slightly see-through. In life it holds a capillary network, a central lymphatic (lacteal) that takes up absorbed fat as chylomicrons, smooth muscle strands and many immune cells.

notes: SubTool-1 = columnar cells with brush border (enterocytes), SubTool-2 = 51 pale cells with basal nuclei (goblet cells), SubTool-0 = sleeve under the epithelium (basement membrane), SubTool-3 = translucent villus core (lamina propria, the file's own alpha 0.82 kept). SubTool-4 = 11 identical spheres with a purple nucleus placed within the epithelium: named intraepithelial lymphocytes by morphology and position (the creator does not label them; the same sphere-with-nucleus design appears in her trachea model). Capillaries, the lacteal, crypts, Paneth and enteroendocrine cells are not modelled. Vertex colours look sRGB-encoded but are read as linear, so the model renders paler than the thumbnail; no colour overrides were used because they would erase the painted nuclei.
